analysis.body:
The U.S. Government Accountability Office reviewed AI implementation across major federal agencies and found that twenty of twenty-three agencies reported approximately 1,200 current and planned AI use cases, while three agencies reported having no uses for AI at all. Of those roughly 1,200 cases, only about 200 represented AI that agencies were actively using in production at the time of review, with the remainder still in planning or exploratory phases. NASA and the Department of Commerce reported the highest numbers of use cases among the agencies surveyed. GAO also found that only five of the fifteen agencies with incomplete records provided comprehensive information for each reported use case, and two agency inventories included items that the agencies themselves later determined were not AI at all, a data quality problem that GAO warned would hinder the government's ability to manage its AI portfolio.

The operational uses that agencies did report cover a range of functions, including analyzing photographs from drones, processing data from cameras and radar to identify border activities, targeting scientific specimens for planetary rovers, identifying information security threats, and facilitating review of large datasets. The President's fiscal year 2023 budget request included 1.8 billion dollars for nondefense research and development investment in AI, signaling continued federal financial commitment even as implementation lags behind policy intent.

On compliance with the legal and executive-order requirements that govern federal AI use, GAO found a mixed picture. Ten of twenty-three agencies implemented all AI requirements specific to their agencies, twelve implemented some but not all, and one was exempt. The Department of Commerce and the General Services Administration stood out as fully implementing selected requirements, with Commerce creating a plan to develop AI technical standards and GSA establishing the AI Center of Excellence. The Office of Management and Budget had not yet developed government-wide guidance on how agencies should acquire and use AI, a gap GAO identified as preventing agencies from consistently managing AI risks and benefits. The Office of Personnel Management had not yet established or updated an occupational category for employees performing AI work, and the Office of Science and Technology Policy had not communicated which agencies were expected to fulfill specific requirements.

Beyond the federal level, the legislative environment is active and accelerating. The law itself is tracked on this site's AI Laws section, which monitors 2,440 AI bills across 53 jurisdictions, updated daily from LegiScan. That volume of legislative activity means any organization operating in or contracting with government must treat the regulatory landscape as a moving target, since requirements can shift substantially from one state or federal session to the next. OECD.AI, the Policy Observatory operated by the OECD, tracks national AI strategies, public-sector initiatives, and ethical frameworks across member and partner countries, providing a reference point for how different governments are structuring governance obligations for AI actors. Oxford Insights produces a Government AI Readiness Index that scores nearly every country on policy capacity, governance, infrastructure, and public-sector adoption, and functions as the standard cross-national comparison tool for assessing where governments stand relative to one another.

Stanford HAI's annual AI Index carries a government and policy track covering legislation counts, national strategy execution, and public-sector procurement, and the 2026 edition notes that the frameworks needed to govern and evaluate AI are falling behind the technology's rate of integration into the broader economy. For a reader considering whether to deploy AI in a government context or to sell AI to government buyers, the practical takeaway from these sources is that federal agencies are moving, but unevenly, that inventory and acquisition guidance gaps create procurement uncertainty, and that the sheer number of active state bills makes jurisdiction-specific legal review a prerequisite rather than an afterthought.
